strengths: Tackles an underexplored and practically relevant problem: panoramic semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid robots under gait-induced jitter, distinct from the dominant forward-facing autonomous-driving setting.

Releases two new benchmarks (QuadOcc: real quadruped 360° data; Human360Occ: CARLA-based human-ego 360° data with RGB/depth/occupancy across 16 maps), which could be useful community resources if released as promised.

The proposed components (DP-ER, BGV, GDC, AMoE-3D) are individually well-motivated with clear geometric/physical rationale (equator-pole trade-off, near/far balance, phase-error correction before lifting, anisotropic panoramic structure).

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: comparisons against both LiDAR-based and vision-based SSC baselines, per-class IoU breakdowns, lighting-condition robustness study, ablations showing additive gains from each module, qualitative figures, and an efficiency/latency analysis relevant to onboard deployment.

Larger relative improvement under the more challenging cross-city (H3O-Heter) setting suggests some genuine robustness benefit from the proposed distortion-aware design, not just overfitting to a single domain.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains on the real-world QuadOcc benchmark are modest (+1.37 mIoU over best vision baseline, +2.12 over best LiDAR baseline), and per-component ablation gains are similarly small (0.26–0.41 mIoU each), raising the question of whether the added architectural complexity (four distinct modules) is fully justified relative to a strong tuned MonoScene baseline.

On the QuadOcc night split, OneOcc actually underperforms MonoScene in mIoU (13.50 vs 14.20), which is not thoroughly analyzed beyond a brief mention of 'precision' advantage; this partially undercuts the robustness narrative central to the paper's motivation.

QuadOcc is limited in scale and diversity (10 scenes, single campus domain, only 6 semantic categories), which limits confidence that reported gains generalize to more varied real-world legged robot deployments; the semi-automatic ground-truth pipeline (multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM + manual fixes) is not independently validated for annotation quality/noise.

Baselines used for comparison (MonoScene 2022, VoxFormer/OccFormer 2023, SGN 2024) are somewhat dated relative to the extensive 2024-2025 related work cited in Section 2 (e.g., panoramic-specific methods like OmniOcc, OccCylindrical, or more recent transformer/Gaussian-based SSC methods); omitting these from quantitative comparison weakens the state-of-the-art claim.

GDC is described as disabled on H3O ('optional on H3O') without a clear explanation of why, which raises questions about the general applicability of this module and slightly weakens the unified-framework narrative.

No cross-dataset generalization experiment (e.g., train on H3O, test on QuadOcc or vice versa) is reported, despite both being introduced as complementary panoramic occupancy benchmarks for legged/humanoid robots; such a study would better support claims of robustness across embodiments/domains.

Reproducibility is not yet verifiable, as code and datasets are stated to be released in the future rather than provided with the submission; some technical details (e.g., precise calibration procedure, number of MoE experts K, training schedule specifics) are only partially specified in the main text.
No reporting of variance across multiple training runs/seeds, making it hard to assess whether the reported margins (some as small as ~0.3 mIoU) are statistically meaningful.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: panoramic, vision-only semantic occupancy prediction for legged/humanoid robots under gait-induced jitter, distinct from the well-trodden forward-facing autonomous-driving SSC setting.

Contributes two new benchmarks (QuadOcc: real quadruped, first-person 360°, day/dusk/night; Human360Occ: CARLA human-ego 360° with RGB/depth/occupancy and within-/cross-city splits), which could be useful community resources if released as promised.

The proposed components (DP-ER dual-projection, BGV bi-grid voxelization, GDC gait compensation, Hierarchical AMoE-3D) are individually well-motivated relative to panoramic geometry and gait dynamics, and the ablation study (Table 4) shows consistent, additive gains as each module is added.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation against both re-trained LiDAR baselines and adapted vision baselines, plus lighting-condition breakdown (day/dusk/night) and an efficiency analysis (latency, parameters, memory) relevant to onboard deployment.
Qualitative results (Fig. 4) are illustrative and support the claimed improvements in boundary sharpness and occlusion handling.
The zero-initialized GDC design (analogous to zero-conv) is a sensible, low-risk mechanism for feature-level motion correction without extra sensors.
weaknesses: QuadOcc is small and geographically narrow (10 scenes, single campus domain, 6 semantic classes at a coarse 64×64×8/0.4 m grid), which limits confidence in generalization claims from this benchmark alone; no cross-domain/cross-campus evaluation is shown for QuadOcc analogous to H3O's cross-city split.

Absolute mIoU gains on QuadOcc are modest (+1.37 over MonoScene, +2.12 over LMSCNet) and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported, so it is hard to assess statistical significance of the improvement over strong baselines.

The paper does not compare against the dedicated panoramic/omnidirectional SSC methods discussed in its own related work (e.g., OmniOcc, cylindrical fusion methods, event-based panoramic SSC); baselines are instead pinhole methods adapted via unwrapping, which may bias the comparison in OneOcc's favor since its design is tailored to this exact adaptation problem.

At night, OneOcc's mIoU underperforms MonoScene (13.50 vs 14.20), a genuine failure case that is only briefly explained qualitatively (frustum-artifact suppression/precision trade-off) without deeper analysis or mitigation.

QuadOcc's ground truth relies on semi-automatic pipeline (multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM initialization + manual fixes); the accuracy/consistency of this labeling process is not quantitatively validated (e.g., no inter-annotator agreement or validation against fully manual subsets), raising some concern about benchmark reliability.

The model is described as 'lightweight' but has 101.76M parameters and ~70ms latency at FP32, which is not obviously lightweight compared to alternatives; the term could be better justified or comparative parameter/FLOP counts for baselines could be shown.
Ablations are performed only on QuadOcc; it is not shown whether the same component-wise gains hold on H3O, leaving open whether the architecture choices are dataset-specific.
The Jetson Thor deployment claim is a simple linear FLOP-based extrapolation rather than measured on-device performance, which weakens the practical deployability claims.
Some motivational claims (e.g., 'hurt the feature→voxel lifting step more than the image→feature step') are stated without direct empirical support isolating this specific claim.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: panoramic single-camera semantic occupancy for legged/humanoid robots subject to gait-induced jitter, distinct from the forward-facing, stable-platform assumptions of most SSC literature.

Contributes two new benchmarks (QuadOcc: real quadruped panoramic data with semi-automatic LiDAR+VLM labeling; Human360Occ: large-scale CARLA-based human-ego panoramic dataset with within-/cross-city splits), which could be useful community resources given the scarcity of panoramic occupancy data.

The proposed components (Dual-Projection ER fusion, Bi-Grid Voxelization, Hierarchical AMoE-3D, Gait Displacement Compensation) are each motivated by specific panoramic/legged-robot geometry considerations (equator-pole distortion trade-off, azimuthal continuity vs. metric fidelity, anisotropic scene structure, motion blur), and the paper provides reasonably clear derivations (Taylor/OCam unwrapping, spherical projections).

Extensive empirical validation: ablations on QuadOcc showing additive gains from each module, plus an unusually thorough supplementary study (FoV scaling, calibration-noise robustness, voxel-resolution trade-offs, temporal aggregation, expert-count ablation, near/far range breakdown, Jetson AGX Orin on-device latency) that substantiates efficiency and robustness claims beyond typical SSC papers.
Reasonable efficiency profile (lightweight decoder, competitive FPS/memory vs. baselines) supporting the paper's stated goal of deployability on payload/power-constrained platforms.

Honest limitations discussion, including a failure-case analysis (vegetation misclassified as sidewalk under rare weather/lighting combinations) and explicit acknowledgment of sim-to-real gap and single-frame limitations.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest (mIoU around 20.56 on QuadOcc, ~32-37 on H3O), and improvements over the best vision baseline on QuadOcc are relatively small (+1.37 mIoU), raising questions about the practical significance of the method beyond H3O, where gains are larger but the data is fully synthetic.

Per-module ablation gains are individually small (+0.26 to +0.41 mIoU each for DP-ER/BGV/AMoE-3D on QuadOcc), and the method adds substantial parameter/compute overhead (e.g., nearly doubling parameters with dual-projection encoders on QuadOcc), so the cost-benefit trade-off of the full pipeline versus simpler baselines is not fully convincing at the main-paper level.

QuadOcc ground truth relies on a semi-automatic pipeline (Grounded-SAM open-vocabulary segmentation + multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + limited manual correction) without a reported quantitative validation (e.g., against manually verified ground truth) of label accuracy/noise, which is a concern given that the benchmark's own quality partly determines the reliability of comparisons.

Human360Occ, which shows the largest reported gains, is purely simulated (CARLA) with an artificial vertical 'bob' as a proxy for gait, so it is unclear how well the demonstrated 'gait robustness' and cross-city generalization transfer to real humanoid/legged motion patterns and real optical/sensor artifacts.

Baseline comparisons are restricted to relatively established SSC methods (MonoScene, VoxFormer, OccFormer, SGN, LMSCNet, SSCNet, OccRWKV); several more recent occupancy methods cited in related work (e.g., GaussianFormer variants, SparseOcc, RenderOcc) are not benchmarked, leaving open whether OneOcc's advantage holds against more modern architectures.

The 'Gait Displacement Compensation' module operates purely on single-frame spatial features (a 2D offset regressed per frame) and is framed as correcting gait-induced motion blur; this is essentially a learned deformable-sampling/anti-aliasing mechanism rather than an explicit temporal or physical gait model, and the qualitative analysis (Fig. 8) is based on only three illustrative examples rather than systematic quantitative validation of the physical claim (e.g., correlation with actual IMU-measured jitter).

The manuscript (with supplementary) is extremely long and dense, with many self-contained ablation studies; while thorough, this can make it harder to assess which findings are core versus incidental, and some claims (e.g., 'sets a new state of the art') are somewhat strong given the narrow margins over vision baselines on the real-world QuadOcc benchmark.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem (panoramic, single-camera semantic occupancy for legged/humanoid robots under gait-induced jitter) rather than yet another autonomous-driving SSC variant.

Two new benchmarks (QuadOcc real-world quadruped, Human360Occ simulated human-ego) are released with detailed construction pipelines, which could be useful to the community regardless of the method's own merits.

Extensive supplementary ablations (expert count, FoV scaling, bi-grid vs single-grid, dual-projection vs single-projection, voxel-resolution scaling, calibration-noise robustness, temporal aggregation) show the authors probed many design axes and report both positive and negative results (e.g., higher resolution hurts mIoU, large K hurts routing).

Reasonable practical framing: parameter/latency/memory accounting, including Jetson AGX Orin on-device numbers, supports the 'lightweight' claims better than most SSC papers that only report desktop-GPU throughput.
weaknesses: Methodological circularity in QuadOcc ground truth: semantic labels are produced by projecting Grounded-SAM (vision-based open-vocabulary segmentation) predictions from the same equirectangular imagery onto aggregated LiDAR points. This raises a real concern that the 'vision-only OneOcc surpasses LiDAR baselines' headline result is partly an artifact of GT being vision-derived, which should systematically favor camera-based predictors and penalize pure-LiDAR baselines whose only route to high score is via geometry that happens to coincide with the vision-based labels. This confound is not discussed or controlled for.

QuadOcc contains only 10 scenes (although 24K frames, these are temporally correlated and drawn from a 'campus domain'), which is a narrow basis for claims of robustness and generalization and raises overfitting/variance concerns for the reported 1.37 mIoU margin over MonoScene -- a difference of this size could plausibly fall within scene-to-scene variability given only 10 scenes.

Absolute accuracy remains low (mIoU in the ~20-37 range even for the proposed method), and per-component ablation gains are individually marginal (+0.26 to +0.41 mIoU per module on QuadOcc), so the architecture's added complexity (four distinct modules: DP-ER, BGV, AMoE-3D, GDC) yields a fairly modest cumulative improvement (19.19→20.56 mIoU, ~7% relative) relative to its engineering overhead.

The 'lightweight' framing is inconsistent: the full Dual-Projection variant used on QuadOcc nearly doubles parameters versus the ER-only variant (101.76M→189.83M) for only +0.53 mIoU, and MonoScene itself is heavier only because its single large 2D encoder is not optimized for the panoramic setting -- the efficiency comparison is somewhat favorable framing rather than a strictly fair efficiency-matched comparison.

Individual technical components are largely adaptations of well-established ideas (cylindrical/polar voxelization à la Cylinder3D/PointOcc, dual raw+unwrapped panorama streams, MoE fusion with gating, zero-initialized offset heads reminiscent of ControlNet/zero-conv) to the panoramic/legged setting, so the architectural novelty is incremental rather than conceptually new.

Baseline adaptation choices (e.g., disabling relation loss, substantially widening LMSCNet/SSCNet channels by 8x, choosing specific BEV positional-encoding resolutions for VoxFormer) are extensively hand-tuned per baseline on the new datasets by the authors themselves, which creates room for implicit bias in baseline retraining even though the intent is described as fairness.

H3O is purely synthetic (CARLA) and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges an unaddressed sim-to-real gap; no real-world human-ego evaluation is provided to validate that the simulated gains transfer to reality.

The main paper's self-contained ablation and analysis content is fairly thin (one QuadOcc-only ablation table) relative to the enormous supplementary material (30+ additional pages), making it hard to assess the core claims without relying heavily on appendix content that would not typically receive the same scrutiny as the main submission.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: panoramic, camera-only semantic occupancy prediction tailored to legged/humanoid robots with gait-induced jitter, rather than simply repurposing autonomous-driving SSC pipelines.

Contributes two new benchmarks (QuadOcc: real quadruped panoramic data with semi-automatic LiDAR+Grounded-SAM labeling across day/dusk/night; Human360Occ: large CARLA-based human-ego panoramic dataset with dual resolutions and within-/cross-city splits), which fill a clear gap in the literature and are likely to be useful to the community.

The proposed components (DP-ER, BGV, GDC, Hierarchical AMoE-3D) are individually well-motivated by panoramic-specific geometric reasoning (equator/pole trade-off, azimuthal continuity, near/far balance) and validated by clean, additive ablations (Table 4).

Extensive supplementary experiments (FoV scaling, resolution scaling, calibration-noise robustness, temporal aggregation, number-of-experts ablation, near/far range analysis, Jetson edge-runtime profiling) substantially strengthen the empirical case and demonstrate the practical, deployable nature of the method.

Results are consistently positive across both benchmarks and across LiDAR and vision baselines, with especially large and robust gains under cross-city/domain-shift conditions on H3O (+8.08 mIoU) and consistent near/far range improvements relevant to robot safety.
Efficiency analysis (parameters, FPS, memory, INT8/FP16 Jetson deployment) is thorough and supports the lightweight/deployability claims rather than just asserting them.
Good scientific transparency: failure case analysis, discussion of limitations (resolution, sim-to-real gap, single-frame design), and societal impact are included rather than omitted.
weaknesses: On QuadOcc, the headline gain over the best vision baseline is modest (+1.37 mIoU / 19.19→20.56), and OneOcc actually underperforms MonoScene at night (13.50 vs 14.20 mIoU), tempering the 'new state of the art' framing for the real-world dataset.

QuadOcc is fairly small in scale (10 scenes, single quadruped platform, campus-only environment) and its ground truth relies on semi-automatic pipelines (multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM initialization + manual fixes), which may introduce label noise not fully quantified beyond a confidence heuristic.

H3O is purely synthetic (CARLA), and while the paper acknowledges the sim-to-real gap as a limitation, no real humanoid panoramic data is used to validate that the simulated benchmark's conclusions transfer to physical humanoid systems.

The overall system integrates many interacting components (dual encoders, dual voxel grids, GDC, MoE decoder), and although ablations are additive and mostly convincing, the cumulative complexity makes some individual design choices (e.g., disabling the relation loss, specific expert count K=4) feel somewhat empirically/heuristically tuned rather than principled.

No direct quantitative comparison is provided against other recently published panoramic/omnidirectional occupancy or humanoid-occupancy methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., OmniOcc, HumanoidPano, RoboOcc), even though these seem closely related; comparisons are limited to adapted standard pinhole SSC baselines.

The claimed 'rivaling LiDAR' framing is somewhat overstated for geometry-only IoU, where LiDAR-based SGN† still achieves higher geometric IoU (49.16) than OneOcc using additional LiDAR input, so the camera-only advantage is specifically in mIoU/semantics rather than uniformly across all metrics.
